an6.30:3.2: The “arched harp” (_vīṇa_) was a multi-stringed instrument held in the lap, whose form is clear from representations in ancient Indian sculptures in Bharhut, Amarāvatī, and Pawāyā, as well as the coins of Samudragupta. The strings, typically seven in number, were attached to the base of the soundbox and passed through holes in the parchment resonator to be tied with cords to the curved neck (these parts are listed at [sn35.246:4.17]()). It accompanied song or dance, and was played equally by men and women. It is not the modern Indian instrument called *veena*, which is a lute or stick zither, but rather is similar to the Burmese *saung*
